A subtitle is something secondary that adds clarity to something primary. The word "sub" means "below" or "under," and that's exactly where subtitles appear — either physically below the main title on a page, or at the bottom of a screen. In both cases, the subtitle's job is the same: to help you understand something better.

The word has two distinct but related meanings depending on the context.
Meaning 1: A Secondary Title for a Written or Creative Work

When a book, article, film, album, podcast, or any creative work has two titles — a main one and an explanatory one — the second, explanatory title is called the subtitle.

Why does this exist?

Main titles are often short, catchy, or poetic. They grab your attention. But they don't always tell you what the work is actually about. The subtitle fills that gap. It tells you the subject, scope, genre, or angle of the work.

How it looks

A subtitle is typically placed right after the main title, separated by a colon.

Main Title: Subtitle

Examples

  • "Sapiens: A Brief History of Humankind"
    • Sapiens is the main title — intriguing, but vague.
    • A Brief History of Humankind is the subtitle — now you know exactly what the book covers.
  • "Educated: A Memoir"
    • Educated is the main title — evocative, but it could mean many things.
    • A Memoir is the subtitle — it tells you the genre (a true personal story).
  • "Thinking, Fast and Slow" ← no subtitle here, the title is self-contained.
  • "The Shallows: What the Internet Is Doing to Our Brains"
    • The Shallows alone gives you little information.
    • The subtitle tells you everything you need to decide whether you want to read it.

Where subtitles appear

  • Books: Almost universally used, especially in nonfiction. Academic books almost always have subtitles because precision matters.
  • Academic research papers: e.g., "Sleep and Memory: How Rest Consolidates Learning"
  • Newspaper and magazine articles: A headline grabs attention; the subtitle (sometimes called a deck or subheadline in journalism) gives the key detail. You see this all the time — a bold main headline followed by a smaller line of text that explains it.
  • Documentary films and TV series: e.g., "Planet Earth II: Islands" — here Planet Earth II is the series title and Islands is the subtitle of that particular episode.
  • Albums and songs: Less common, but musicians sometimes use them.

What a subtitle does and doesn't do

A subtitle clarifies and supports — it never replaces the main title. The main title is still the primary name of the work. The subtitle is a helper. If someone asks "what book are you reading?", you'd say Sapiens, not the subtitle.
Meaning 2: Text Displayed on Screen During a Video, Film, or Show

This is probably the more commonly known meaning in everyday life today.

Subtitles are lines of text that appear — usually at the bottom of a screen — to show viewers what is being said (or sometimes written) in a video.

Why subtitles exist

Imagine you're watching a film made in Spanish, but you don't speak Spanish. How do you understand what's happening? The filmmakers add subtitles — a translation of the spoken dialogue, displayed as text on screen, so you can read along while watching. This is their most traditional purpose.

But subtitles are used in many other situations too:

  • For deaf and hard-of-hearing viewers: Subtitles let them follow the dialogue they cannot hear.
  • For language learners: Watching a show with subtitles in the target language helps learners connect spoken words to their written form.
  • In noisy environments: Watching a video on a crowded train or in a loud café? Subtitles let you follow along even without sound.
  • For strong accents or unclear speech: Even when dialogue is in your own language, subtitles can help you catch every word.
  • For concentration and comprehension: Many people find they absorb content better when they can both hear and read it simultaneously.

How subtitles work on screen

  • They appear as short lines of text at the bottom of the frame (occasionally at the top, if something important is happening at the bottom).
  • They are synchronized with the audio — the text appears and disappears in time with the speech.
  • They break long sentences into shorter, readable chunks so your eyes can keep up.
  • When multiple people are speaking and it's not obvious who is saying what, subtitles sometimes include the speaker's name: [John]: I'll meet you at the station.
  • They often indicate non-speech sounds when relevant: [door creaks] or [phone ringing].

Open subtitles vs. closed subtitles

  • Open subtitles (also called burned-in or hardcoded subtitles) are permanently part of the video image. You cannot turn them off. They're common in films shown in foreign countries and in older films.
  • Closed subtitles are optional — the viewer can switch them on or off. This is what you do when you go to Settings on Netflix or a YouTube video and toggle subtitles. The video itself doesn't have them baked in; they're a separate layer you activate.

Subtitles vs. closed captions — are they the same?

These two terms are often used interchangeably in everyday speech, and in many parts of the world they're treated as synonyms. But there is a technical distinction worth knowing:

  • Subtitles traditionally assume that the viewer can hear the audio. They primarily translate or transcribe spoken dialogue. They might not mention background music or sound effects because the viewer is assumed to hear those anyway.
  • Closed captions are designed for viewers who cannot hear the audio. They include everything audible: spoken dialogue, yes — but also descriptions of sound effects ([thunder rumbles]), music ([upbeat piano music playing]), tone of voice ([whispering]), etc.

In practice, many platforms use the word "subtitles" to mean both. When you see "CC" (Closed Captions) on your remote or screen, it's doing the job of subtitles too. The distinction matters most in professional, legal, or accessibility contexts.

Subtitles vs. dubbing

Subtitles are one way to make foreign-language content accessible. The alternative is dubbing — replacing the original spoken audio with a new recording in another language. Subtitles let you hear the original voices and performance; dubbing replaces them. Neither is universally "better" — different countries and viewers prefer different approaches.

Both meanings of subtitle share the same underlying logic: a subtitle is a secondary piece of text that exists to help you understand the primary thing better.

For a book, the primary thing is the main title → the subtitle explains it.
For a video, the primary thing is the spoken dialogue → the subtitle makes it accessible.

In both cases, the subtitle never replaces what it supports. It simply makes it clearer.

ContextWhat "subtitle" means
Books, articles, films, albumsA secondary title below the main title, adding explanation or detail
Videos, films, TV shows, online contentText displayed on screen showing what is being spoken or heard

The word is very flexible, but once you know its core logic — secondary text that clarifies the primary thing — every use of it will make immediate sense to you.
